source.title: Polysemantic Dropout: Conformal OOD Detection for Specialized LLMs
source.authors: Ayush Gupta; Ramneet Kaur; Anirban Roy; Adam D. Cobb; Rama Chellappa; Susmit Jha

record.tranche_reason: The paper motivates its OOD-detection method with polysemanticity and redundancy, but reports results for the method and dropout tolerance rather than testing whether neurons encode multiple unrelated concepts or why they do.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses polysemanticity and redundancy as motivation. Its own neuron-dropout results measure response changes under dropout, not the semantic selectivity, prevalence, or cause of polysemantic neurons. Those dropout-response measurements are recorded as findings that fit none of the listed versions; OOD-detection AUROCs are not rows because they report the proposed method's performance, not polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The paper invokes polysemanticity and redundancy only as motivation for a dropout-tolerance OOD detector. It never measures whether any neuron responds to multiple unrelated concepts, how common that is, or why. Its results are AUROCs of its own method plus dropout response-change rates, which are a different construct (robustness to ablation).
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that dropout tolerance, aggregated across layers with valid p-value merging, is an effective conformal non-conformity measure for OOD detection in medical-specialized LLMs (EYE-LLaMA, MentaLLaMA). It beats baselines with AUROC gains of up to 37% while keeping false-alarm guarantees. Polysemanticity is a motivating hypothesis, not a tested conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses neuron dropout as part of a new conformal OOD-detection method; it does not reproduce the original sources' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Dropout response-change rates vary by layer and by the maximum number of neurons dropped; the query groups differ in their share of MCQs.

fits_no_version.finding: In EYE-LLaMA, dropping up to 30 top-activated last-token neurons changes responses for 91%, 74% and 56% of EyeQA calibration queries at layers 7, 15 and 22. MCQ responses change with fewer dropped neurons than subjective queries.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM outputs are more sensitive to ablating highly activated neurons in earlier layers and on choice-based queries than in later layers or on open-ended queries.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The paper does not directly measure neuron polysemanticity. Its dropout-response results are an indirect operational proxy for robustness, and the reported dropout ablations concern EYE-LLaMA and EyeQA rather than testing the listed claim versions. The authors also note that the score is undefined when responses do not change within the maximum dropout limit.
record.rows_left_out: OOD-detection AUROCs, merging-function comparisons, and false-alarm results were left out because they report the proposed method's performance or guarantees rather than results about polysemanticity or neuron semantic selectivity (Sections 4.5–4.6, Tables 1–2, Figures 3–4, and Appendix Figure 6).

untested.parts: There is no measure of what share of LLM MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, nor by layer.
Superposition is cited as the hypothesized cause, but this is not tested.
No architecture, activation or regularization comparison of polysemanticity.
No examination of whether neurons encode one shared feature.
No examination of activation ranges or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T4 / uses_without_test classification is correct. Rows R4–R6 and R10 are method-design or fallback statistics; R7–R9 describe query composition. None bears on any version, so all row states should be cannot_determine rather than observed. Omitting the AUROC tables was appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: Whether vision-model neurons respond to unrelated image inputs.
Whether a large share of language-model MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how this varies by layer.
Whether superposition or feature capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
Whether initialization, regularization, or training noise causes polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
Whether architecture, activation, or regularization changes polysemanticity, or whether it can be lowered without a large performance loss.
Whether apparent polysemantic neurons have a shared feature or related jobs when examined with better tools.
Whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: EYE-LLaMA
rows.operation_detail: Dropped up to 30 maximally activated neurons and measured whether the response changed.
rows.measure: Responses changed within the stated dropout limit
rows.note: A dropout-response result; it does not establish whether the affected neurons encode multiple concepts.
rows.check: The measure is the share of responses changed after dropping up to 30 top-activated neurons, which says nothing about neuron polysemanticity. 'observed' has no version to be observed against. Measure wording should read 'responses changed' (91% changed); it is correct as written.

rows.subject: EYE-LLaMA
rows.operation_detail: Dropped up to 30 maximally activated neurons and measured whether the response changed.
rows.measure: Responses changed within the stated dropout limit
rows.note: A dropout-response result; it does not establish whether the affected neurons encode multiple concepts.
rows.check: Same as R1: a dropout-sensitivity rate (74% changed, layer 15), not a polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: EYE-LLaMA
rows.operation_detail: Dropped up to 30 maximally activated neurons and measured whether the response changed.
rows.measure: Responses changed within the stated dropout limit
rows.note: The paper reports that response changes occur less often in this later layer; this is not a measure of polysemanticity.
rows.check: Same as R1: a dropout-sensitivity rate (56% changed, layer 22). The layer trend concerns sensitivity to ablation, not V2's layer variation in polysemanticity.

rows.subject: EYE-LLaMA
rows.operation_detail: Varied the maximum number of dropped neurons and measured response changes.
rows.measure: Queries with responses changed within the dropout limit
rows.note: The paper says a higher maximum is more likely to change a response.
rows.check: This is a tuning ablation of the method's hyperparameter m (59% changed at m=10). It is closer to a method-design result than a finding about the phenomenon.

rows.check: A method hyperparameter ablation (78% at m=30). The authors chose this value as the operating setting, so it functions as a selection value.

rows.subject: EYE-LLaMA
rows.operation_detail: Used the default in-distribution prediction when no layer yielded a defined score after neuron dropout.

rows.note: The default prediction was in-distribution; the authors state this occurred very rarely.
